title: Personal hygiene, clean work clothing and staying away when unwell
audience: Cleaning and support workers in healthcare, aged care and clinical settings, including agency staff who may not know local rules.
learningOutcomes: Describe the personal hygiene routine expected before and during a shift.
Explain how work clothing is kept clean and how a soiled uniform is handled.
State when a worker must not attend work and whom to tell.

instruction.heading: Personal hygiene is part of the barrier
instruction.body: You are a route that organisms can take, so your own hygiene counts as an infection control measure. The guide sets out a daily routine: shower with soap or body wash, wear clean clothing each day, use deodorant, brush the teeth and floss daily, keep nails clean and short, cover the nose and mouth during coughs and sneezes, and discard used tissues straight away. Mouthwash and cleaning the hands after a smoking break are also listed. Hand hygiene is the most important step and is covered in full in “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”, so it is not repeated here.

instruction.heading: Clean clothing and uniforms
instruction.body: Work clothing should be clean when each shift begins. Keep two or more days of clean clothing on hand so a change is always possible. If a uniform becomes soiled, change it straight away and avoid wearing it for the rest of the shift. An apron worn over the uniform reduces how often that happens. Where the facility supplies scrubs or other hospital clothing, the guide says it should be laundered on site, so that it does not pick up organisms at home, in the car or on public transport. Where you work in the community, you usually wash your own clothing, and some facilities ask for personal clothing to be bagged and taken home for laundering. Follow the procedure your employer gives you, and treat stains with the stain removal method it sets.

instruction.heading: Staying away when unwell
instruction.body: A worker who has a transmissible infection should not come to work or go out in public while infectious. The guide applies this to workers with a cough or fever, and it applies to any transmissible illness. Tell your supervisor before the shift starts, because a late call leaves the team short and may expose residents or patients. Do not diagnose yourself and do not give advice to colleagues. Follow your employer illness procedure and any return-to-work requirement. Agency staff should ask on arrival at each placement, because policies differ between sites.

instruction.heading: Where this sits with the rest of your work
instruction.body: Personal hygiene supports the cleaning methods described in other lessons, but it does not replace them. A clean uniform does not protect a surface you have not cleaned, and a clean surface does not protect a person when the hands touching it are dirty. Keep all parts of the routine in place every shift.

procedure: Shower and dress in clean clothing before the shift, and confirm a clean spare set is on hand.
Before starting, check that your clothing is clean. Change it if it is soiled, and bag it as the facility procedure requires.
Cover coughs and sneezes using a tissue or, failing that, the crook of the elbow, and put used tissues straight into a bin.
Check yourself for symptoms before the shift. If symptoms are present, tell your supervisor and follow the illness procedure before you start.
Launder and store uniforms as the facility requires, and do not take them home where the facility asks you to laundry on site.

workedExamples.situation: A worker wakes with a fever and a cough before a morning shift in a residential aged care home.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not attend. Phone the supervisor before the shift, follow the illness procedure, and follow any return-to-work rule the employer sets. Staying away protects residents and colleagues, and it is the expected step.

workedExamples.situation: During a spill clean-up, a cleaner gets body fluid splashed on the sleeve of a uniform.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What happens to the uniform, and what must be reported?
workedExamples.reasoning: Change the uniform as soon as the task ends, bag it in the soiled-linen process for the facility (see “Soiled and clean linen: handling and storage”), and clean your hands. Report the splash under the exposure procedure in “Body fluid exposure: first response and reporting”.

equipmentAndPpe: Clean uniform or work clothing, and a spare set
Soiled-linen bag or the facility procedure for personal clothing
Tissues and a bin for used tissues

commonErrors.error: Working while unwell because the shift is short of staff.
commonErrors.prevention: Report early. A short-staffed shift is still safer than a worker who spreads an infection.

commonErrors.error: Taking a soiled uniform home on public transport when the facility asks for on-site laundry.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the laundry rule the facility gives you for that uniform.

commonErrors.error: Wearing the same clothing for two days.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep two or more days of clean clothing so a change is always possible.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Follow the workplace illness and return-to-work rules. This lesson does not replace them.
Do not give medical advice to colleagues or to clients about a symptom.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner describes the daily hygiene routine and names at least five items in it.
Learner states the rule for a soiled uniform and the rule for keeping spare clothing.
Learner names the person to tell when unwell before a shift.
documentationEvidence: Record of an absence notified before a shift, with the time and the person told.
Record of any soiled uniform change that followed an exposure, cross-referenced to the exposure record.
summary: Personal hygiene is an infection control measure, and daily routine matters.
Work clothing should be clean when each shift begins, and soiled clothing is changed at once.
A worker with a transmissible illness stays away and tells the supervisor before the shift.

knowledgeChecks.question: When must a worker with a cough and fever stay away from work?
options: Only if the cough is severe and the fever has gone down for a day
Until the employer illness procedure says the worker can return
Once the worker has taken a tablet and feels better for an hour
Only on days when no residents are present and only in the car park

knowledgeChecks.question: How many days of clean work clothing should a worker have available?
Why should a uniform that must be laundered on site not be taken home?
options: Because it costs more to wash and the cost is shared by the team
Because it can pick up organisms on the journey and at home
Because uniforms cannot be cleaned at a residence
Because the laundry rule only applies to scrubs today
